extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners interpreting §101 guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying Step 2B of the Alice/Mayo two-part test: identify additional claim elements beyond a judicial exception and determine whether those elements, individually and in combination, amount to an inventive concept (i.e., 'significantly more').

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding 'apply it' or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent) with the judicial exception, or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, is not enough to qualify as 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include a limitation indicating that a particular function (such as creating and maintaining electronic records) is performed by a computer (Alice Corp., 134 S. Ct. at 2360). See MPEP § 2106.05(f). Such post-hoc recitation of a generic computer performing generic functions does not provide an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities at high level is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry, specified at a high level of generality, does not amount to significantly more than a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that requires no more than a generic computer to perform generic computer functions that are well-understood, routine and conventional is insufficient (Alice Corp., 134 S. Ct. at 2359-60). See MPEP § 2106.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering) to the judicial exception does not supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a step of obtaining information about credit card transactions so the information can be analyzed by an abstract mental process (CyberSource v. Retail Decisions, Inc.). See MPEP § 2106.05(g). Mere pre- or post-solution activity that does not meaningfully limit the exception fails Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linking the exception to a particular technological environment or field of use is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (e.g., hedging in commodities markets or limiting a formula to petrochemical fields) is not 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely specifying a field of use or technological environment does not supply an inventive concept (Bilski; Parker v. Flook). See MPEP § 2106.05(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicality/tangibility is not a relevant consideration in Step 2B
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element or elements is not, by itself, a relevant consideration in Step 2B and does not guarantee eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court explained that a computer's physical existence is 'beside the point' — physical implementation alone cannot convert an ineligible abstract idea into a patent-eligible application (Alice Corp.). Likewise, physical steps (e.g., DNA amplification) do not automatically provide an inventive concept (Genetic Technologies Ltd. v. Merial LLC). Conversely, non-physical elements likewise may not doom claims (Enfish; McRO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B procedure: identify additional elements and evaluate individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must identify any additional elements beyond the judicial exception(s) and evaluate those additional elements both individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This evaluation should reference the Supreme Court's relevant considerations as discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(h). The test is not a weighing test — it is important to evaluate significance relative to what the applicant has invented (consult entire disclosure and apply broadest reasonable interpretation). Considerations may overlap; not all will be relevant to every claim. Claims should be examined separately (one claim might be ineligible while a dependent claim is eligible). If a claim clearly recites multiple discrete exceptions, an examiner may select one and conduct the analysis for that selected exception for efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-as-a-whole requirement: claim must amount to significantly more to be eligible (Pathway C)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim to be eligible under Step 2B, the claim as a whole must amount to significantly more than the judicial exception; if not, the claim is not patent-eligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more, it is eligible at Pathway C and the eligibility analysis is complete. If there are no meaningful limitations that transform the exception into a patent-eligible application, the claim is not eligible and should be rejected (see MPEP § 2106.07 for formulating rejections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to the functioning of a computer or to any other technology/technical field can show an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claim purports to improve the functioning of the computer itself or any other technology or technical field — such an improvement may demonstrate an inventive concept and support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the search for a technological solution to a technological problem (Alice; DDR Holdings; Amdocs). Examiners may evaluate improvement considerations at Step 2A or Step 2B. To show an improvement, the specification should provide a technical explanation sufficient for a person of ordinary skill to recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement (discuss technical problem, unconventional technical solution, or technical improvements over the prior art). After consulting the specification, the claim must itself reflect the improvement (consider full scope under BRI and evaluate the claim as a whole as an ordered combination without oversimplifying).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to computer functionality: distinguishing true computer improvements from mere computer implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: In computer-related technologies, determine whether the claim purports to improve computer capabilities (a true technical improvement) or merely invokes a computer as a tool to perform conventional or abstract processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have recognized improvements where the specification and claim focus on improving how computers store/retrieve data, distribute functionality, render images, reduce congestion, provide particular memory system structures, specific transmission techniques, server structures, or particular software designs (Enfish; BASCOM; Research Corp.; Amdocs; Visual Memory; TLI; Apple v. Ameranth). Conversely, claims whose entire scope can be performed mentally or verbally, or that merely automate manual processes using generic computers, are not improvements (Synopsys; RecogniCorp; FairWarning; Return Mail; Credit Acceptance; LendingTree; TLI). Examples that may show improvement: modification of hyperlink protocol (DDR), inventive distribution of network functionality (BASCOM), halftone rendering (Research Corp.), unconventional distributed network arch. (Amdocs), configurable memory (Visual Memory), technical details for image transmission (TLI), particular server structure for storing organized digital images (TLI), particular software/menu programming (Apple). Examples that may not suffice include menu generation (Ameranth), mere speed increases from general-purpose computers (FairWarning), using a computer to perform an abstract idea (Return Mail), mere automation of manual processes (Credit Acceptance; LendingTree), and conventional digital image handling (TLI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to non-computer technologies may also demonstrate eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements in other technologies or technical fields (beyond pure computer-functionality improvements) can demonstrate patent eligibility when the claim describes a particular way to solve a technical problem or an improvement in an existing technological process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples the courts have indicated may be sufficient include: computerized methods of operating industrial machinery (Diamond v. Diehr), new telephone/server combinations (TLI), advances in downloading/streaming (Affinity Labs), improved digital compression methods (DDR/Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec), virus screening incorporated into the Internet (Symantec), measurement devices generating new data (Electric Power Group v. Alstom), and particular sensor configurations and their methods of use (Thales Visionix). The claim and specification should convey the particular technical solution rather than merely the idea of a solution or outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept may arise from non-conventional, non-generic arrangement of elements (consider combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if individual additional elements are known and conventional, their non-conventional and non-generic arrangement as claimed may together supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BASCOM illustrates that a remote filtering tool installed at a specific location with customizable features for each end user — an arrangement of known components — yielded an inventive concept when considered as an ordered combination. Thus examiners must consider both individual elements and their combination; inventive concept can be found in the claimed arrangement.
